comments.author: jamesbelchamber
comments.story: How often do full-body MRIs find cancer?
comments.why: Good video on why screening catches more cancer without saving more people.
comments.text: It does, doesn't it! This is basically the reason scepticism in screening has risen (amongst scientists and medics, not the general population) - research seems to show that screening catches much more cancer but doesn't save many more people. Rohin Francis does a good video on it, which you don't have to watch because it has references underneath you can click straight through to (the video is good though): [VIDEO] I am frustrated by this because it seems obvious to me that "more data == better" but I guess it makes sense if you think of the scans as having high amounts of noise, and us having a poor understanding of the system we're monitoring (this never happens in tech, of course :)).

comments.why: Shows early detection is not straightforward; US versus UK prostate survival.
comments.text: Compare and contrast this video from 'Medlife Crisis': [VIDEO] > Trying to detect disease early seems like an obviously good thing to do. But reality isn't always quite so straightforward, especially in medicine. If It Ducks Like A Quack is a series where I try to go beyond the hype and explore how complicated the apparently simple phenomena in medicine are. One point from the video: five year survival rates of prostate cancer in the US are massively better than in the UK. However, roughly the same proportion of people die of prostate cancer in both countries. The US just screens a lot more.

comments.author: rdedev
comments.story: Most cancer screenings don’t extend life, study finds
comments.why: Screening not benign; positives can lead to unnecessary interventions.
comments.text: I think the consensus on cancer screening is stil not fully there? Came across this video by a cardiologist a long time ago [VIDEO] I guess the main gist is that screening is not completely benign and a positive screen might lead to more interventions for what in the end could just be a benign tumor. Then there's the other point of detecting it late in life. Like treatment for cancer might not make much sense if you are already 89 years old
